content:
I spent a day reading kaggriculture.py rather than the README, and the thing that surprised me most is that the base-price table ranks the products almost exactly backwards.

The price function is base ± amp · f(|inv − I0|), and the two sides of I0 are separate curves with separate shapes and separate steepness. Selling pushes inventory up the glut side. The town — the town centre once a day, plus shops every four turns — pulls it down the scarcity side, for free, all season.

So a product has two values, and which one you get depends only on timing. Selling the season's output of each product into the hole the town has dug, versus dumping the same quantity into an untouched market:

product base town eats into the hole dumped flat
STRAWBERRY 120 426 $100,445 $4,173
MILK 160 327 $86,662 $6,432
WOOL 200 228 $54,340 $8,097
WHEAT 25 525 $21,152 $10,813
TOMATO 60 228 $16,812 $7,861
CARROT 35 327 $13,246 $6,904
EGG 50 228 $12,972 $9,658
MELON 250 30 $8,184 $7,416

Strawberry, the fourth-most expensive item on the board, is worth 24× more sold late than sold early, and it is the biggest market in the game. Melon, the most expensive, is the smallest — no shop buys melon. Check the eight shop menus in SHOPS: bakery, pizza shop, brunch spot, yarn store, ice cream shop, pet cafe, smoothie shop, farmers market. Melon appears on none of them, so its only sink is the town centre's one per day, thirty for the whole season. And its glut curve is squared with a target of 3.6, which puts it on the $1 floor after 158 units.

Two more things that fell out of the same arithmetic:

Per tile, animals dominate and strawberry does not. A strawberry plant yields four units in seventeen days; a cow yields 1.5 milk a day for twenty-two days once you count the CARE bonus, plus a free fertilizer daily. Allocating tiles greedily by marginal revenue, the first fifteen are all cows and sheep, melon enters around tile sixteen, and strawberry only earns about thirteen tiles out of a hundred. It is the best thing to sell and a mediocre thing to grow.

Labour is not a constraint. HIRE costs fib(n) and the counter resets every morning, so ten hands cost $143 for 230 extra actions. What is a constraint is walking: my first agent spent 83% of all unit-turns moving, because it recomputed each hand's target every turn and they thrashed. Making a unit finish the tile it stands on before moving — FEED, CARE, HARVEST, COLLECT_FERTILIZER are all done from the same square — took that to 55% and roughly tripled the final bank.

I wrote all of this up with the charts and a working reference agent here: https://www.kaggle.com/code/nekkon/strawberry-pays-24x-what-the-price-table-says — everything is computed from the installed market_price and SHOPS rather than retyped from the README, so the numbers are checkable by rerunning the cells.

Caveat worth stating plainly: the drain figures assume the expected number of each shop type, since shops are drawn with replacement and a season can end up with three bakeries and no yarn store. And the whole thing assumes an opponent selling at a similar rate — the hole is shared, and against a passive opponent these numbers roughly double. My own agent still loses to the best public ones by about 4×, mostly on scale, so treat the analysis as more solid than the executor.

Corrections very welcome, especially on the drain schedule.

Your drain schedule is right, and I can offer an independent check on it since you asked. Deriving it from SHOPS, TOWN_CENTER_PRODUCTS and townShopSellInterval = 4 instead of by simulation, I get the same nine numbers you do: 525 wheat, 426 strawberry, 327 carrot and milk, 228 tomato, egg and wool, 30 melon, 0 fertilizer. The mechanism that fixes it is that shops unlock at the end of day d when (d+1) % 3 == 0 and cap at 8, which comes to 132 shop-instance-days over a 30 day season. Two different routes to the same table is about as much confirmation as this kind of arithmetic can get. Taking the same route further, your drain table is exactly the input needed for a closed-form ceiling on the total money in an episode: about $703k at median demand for both players combined, and across 32,570 public episodes none exceeds it, with the best game on record collecting 48% of it. Which says the market's willingness to pay is not what stops an agent here, and lines up with your own note that your analysis is more solid than your executor.

One thing worth knowing, because it moves part of your ranking: your table is a 1.32.6 table. On 1.32.7 carrot, tomato and egg had their scarcity branch changed to a hinge, linear up to a knee at T then + 8.0 * (scarcity/T - 1)**2. So exactly the three lines near the bottom of your "into the hole" column now pay very differently at depth. Carrot at a scarcity of 1,000 goes from $43 a unit to $531. Carrot also got a second change the announcement does not mention, below_target from 0.20 to 1.00, which lifts its curve below the knee as well.

How much that is actually worth is less than those numbers suggest, and it took percentiles rather than a maximum to see it. Dumping 100 units at the scarcity real games reach, measured over 120 recorded episodes: carrot is 1.35x the old revenue at the median game, 2.00x at p90, and 9.56x only in the single deepest game of the 120. Tomato is 1.00x at the median to the dollar and 1.98x at p90. Egg is 1.00x at the median, at p75, and 1.06x at p90, so despite firing in a quarter of games it does not reach the money. The firing rates and the payoffs rank the three lines differently: rate says tomato, size says carrot.

Your melon point survives all of it untouched. Melon is in 0 of 8 shop menus, its demand is exactly 30 on every seed I have checked, and its curve was not touched, so its deepest scarcity across 160 replayed episodes is 11 units against a knee of 300. It is the only line the scarcity branch cannot reach, which is the mirror image of your observation that it is the smallest market.

On animals dominating per tile, I think your case is stronger than you made it. _daily_refresh_animals sets fertilizer_available = True on every surviving animal every day whether or not you fed it, and uncollected fertilizer does not accumulate, so the stream is worth about 2,900 a season against 1,300 to 1,760 for the milk, eggs or wool the animal is named for. Pricing fertilizer as a by-product undervalues livestock roughly threefold.

Your caveat about the hole being shared is the one I would keep front and centre. Selling harder costs me about $4k and costs the opponent about $11.8k in my own measurements, so the asymmetry runs in the direction you would want but the totals move for both sides.

One last thing, and it is the reason I would not tune an executor against the revenue column at all. Every number in your table and mine maximises money, and money is not what the leaderboard pays. Maximising the expected margin is provably the wrong objective in a two-player duel like this: the right one is a signal to noise ratio, Pr[win] = Φ(μ/σ), which fits the public episodes at a mean absolute error of 0.068. The two disagree in a specific and actionable way, because when you are behind, adding variance helps and adding median does not. I wrote the derivation and the calibration up in Wins, not money. Given you say the analysis is ahead of the executor, that gap may be part of why.

I have checked the installed 1.32.7 source. MARKET_PARAMS reads:

CARROT: below_func "hinge", below_target 1.00,  T 450
TOMATO: below_func "hinge", below_target 0.40,  T 200
EGG:    below_func "hinge", below_target 0.40,  T 332
HINGE_GAIN = 8.0

So my table is a 1.32.6 table, as you say. Recomputing all of it on 1.32.7:

old 1.32.7 change
CARROT $13,246 $15,614 +18%
TOMATO $16,812 $16,849 +0.2%
EGG $12,972 $12,972 0%

Everything else is unchanged to the dollar and the ranking does not move.

The parameters predict your percentiles. The quadratic term is 8.0 * max(0, x/T - 1)**2, identically zero below the knee, so the only thing that matters is the knee against the season's own expected scarcity:

CARROT   knee T=450   season drain 327   0.73x knee   never reaches it
TOMATO   knee T=200   season drain 228   1.14x knee   barely crosses
EGG      knee T=332   season drain 228   0.69x knee   never reaches it

Two of the three cannot fire at median demand — the town does not eat enough of them in thirty days to get there. That is your 1.00x median for egg and your 1.00x-to-the-dollar for tomato, derived instead of measured.

For carrot, the hinge is not what moved it. Holding scarcity at the season's actual 327 and swapping one parameter at a time:

carrot unit price at scarcity 327
old: sqrt, below_target 0.20 $41
hinge, below_target 0.20 $40
sqrt, below_target 1.00 $65
new: hinge, below_target 1.00 $60

The hinge alone is worth minus one dollar. The whole move is the below_target change you mention in passing, and since the announcement omits it, that is the headline rather than the footnote. The hinge only takes over past 450, which is where your p90 and your deepest game live.

Fertilizer: confirmed, and I understated it. _daily_refresh_animals sets fertilizer_available = True on every surviving animal after the escape check, regardless of fed_today, and COLLECT_FERTILIZER clears it with no accumulation.

The valuation has a wrinkle, though, and it is my own post's trap mirrored. Fertilizer is the one product with a town drain of exactly zero — no shop menu lists it, the town centre skips it — so there is no hole to sell it into and every unit prices on the glut branch, about $98 and degrading slowly. Milk sold into its hole is $86,662 over 327 units, or $265/unit. Per unit the named product is 2.7x fertilizer until the shared 327-unit hole is exhausted, after which milk drops to its own glut branch and your ranking is the right one. Fertilizer is the low-variance income, the product is the high-variance one — which bears on your last point.

On wins versus money I have no counterargument. Both our tables maximise margin, the leaderboard pays Pr[win] = Φ(μ/σ), and the two disagree exactly where it is actionable: behind, variance helps and median does not. I never questioned the objective. I'll work through your derivation before touching the executor again.

The notebook computes every number from the installed market_price and SHOPS and pip-installs the engine with --upgrade, so a re-run regenerates those three lines on 1.32.7 by itself; the frozen table in the post above is the stale artifact, not the notebook. Re-running it now with the knee-versus-drain comparison added, credited to this thread

Late to this, and destbreso has already done the confirmation I was going to offer: I derived your town-eats column the same way and got the same nine numbers, and his 132 shop-instance-days is the same arithmetic. So instead, three things that are about the spread rather than the mean, plus one disagreement.

Your column and his are the expected value. The draw around it is wide enough to change decisions. Eight shops, uniform with replacement, so the median season opens 5 distinct types out of 8. Median season demand: wheat 504, strawberry 396, milk 288, carrot 270, and 180 each for tomato, wool and egg. The part I would plan around is the zero row. Wool sits on one menu, so 34% of seasons have no wool buyer at all. Carrot is zero in 10% of seasons and around 684 at the 95th percentile. Your caveat about assuming expected shop counts was the right caveat. On wool it is the difference between a plan and a coin flip.

Second, a benchmarking trap I walked into while measuring that. The shop draw is not independent of play. The engine rolls once per empty tile, for both farms, from the same stream that then picks the shop, so the number of empty tiles on either board moves your town. Same 12 seeds, two different bots: the unlocked shop list differed on all 12. Two versions of my own bot: identical on all 12, though a bigger edit still moved it on 1 seed in 12. Editing your own bot usually keeps the town as a control. Benchmarking against somebody else's loses it, and their play moves your draw as much as yours does.

Third, your walking result, which I think is the most useful thing in your post. I get 32.8% of unit turns spent moving and 16.3% passing, leaving barely half for work. That is against your fixed 55%, not the 83% you started from, and my bot is one farmer on six adjacent tiles, so it should be near the bottom of the range. A third looks like the floor for a compact single-unit layout.

Where I disagree, and I am now disagreeing with both of you: melon. You rank it last and destbreso confirms its demand is exactly 30 with a curve the scarcity branch cannot reach. All true. But I took a six-tile bot, changed two constants, the crop and the harvest day, and nothing else, and it banks +11,665 more than the carrot version, standard error 558, ahead on 8 seeds out of 8 on 1.32.7, both arms against the built-in starter on the same seeds. The bot sells 72 melons against a 30-unit sink, so it does overshoot, but by 42 net units, and melon does not reach the one-coin floor until 158 net. It closes at 232 against a base of 250. Smallest market and worst crop are not the same thing at six tiles.

The draw distribution is in section 10 and the melon measurement in section 15: https://www.kaggle.com/code/georgymamarin/kaggriculture-visualized-what-every-crop-pays
